tldr: The authors introduce a high-force three-finger robotic hand and a task suite tailored for contact-rich "removal manipulation"—such as peeling off adhered objects and scraping stubborn residue. By aligning fingertip forces into a shared wrist-centered frame for imitation learning, policies acquire robust adaptive behaviors from just 20 demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overview of removal manipulation and the proposed framework. (a) Real-robot demonstration of detaching an adhered barnacle model from a turtle mock-up. (b) Human removal behaviors including edge prying and surface scraping. (c) The pipeline: local fingertip sensor forces are geometrically transformed into a shared wrist frame, then fed alongside vision, proprioception, and fingertip poses into an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) for closed-loop control.
overview:
When robots operate in everyday or outdoor environments, they inevitably encounter separation and cleaning tasks: peeling stickers, scraping away stuck debris, or excavating buried items. Unlike standard pick-and-place, these targets are adhered, embedded, or mechanically constrained. They require an initial detachment phase known as "removal manipulation." Crucial properties like adhesive strength, friction, and deformation cannot be fully inferred from camera images or joint angles alone, making force feedback indispensable.

To address this challenge, the authors developed DexRemo, a platform featuring a high-force three-finger robotic hand equipped with modular fingertips and three-axis fingertip force sensing. A central question is how to represent multi-finger force measurements for the policy network. As fingers articulate, their local fingertip sensor frames rotate relative to one another. Using raw local coordinates means identical physical forces end up with vastly different numerical values depending on finger posture. The authors propose a simple, elegant geometric solution: map each fingertip force into a common wrist-centered frame using forward kinematics before feeding it to the learning model.

For real-robot evaluation, they designed a nine-scenario task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. Policies were trained via imitation learning using an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) from just 20 teleoperated demonstrations per task. Controlled ablation experiments across six core benchmark tasks revealed that pairing wrist-frame forces with fingertip poses achieves a dramatically higher success rate (83% core task average vs. 24% to 55% for baselines) and substantially better generalization compared to no-force and local-frame baselines.
contributions: Developed a low-cost, high-power-density three-finger hand platform featuring up to 62.5 N of pull-out force to withstand tough detachment and cleaning, along with modular quick-swap nail/cleaning tips and integrated three-axis fingertip force sensors.

Constructed a real-robot removal manipulation task suite of nine scenarios across adhesive detachment, surface cleaning, and occluded retrieval, establishing strict physical success criteria and held-out test conditions.

Introduced a geometric force representation that expresses three-axis fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, producing a consistent spatiotemporal force feature space and proving via real-robot ablations that it enables robust behavioral adaptation from only 20 demonstrations.

sections.heading: Peeling, Scraping, and Digging: Why "Removal Manipulation" Challenges Robots
sections.summary: When targets are adhered, embedded, or mechanically constrained, robots must break contacts before any standard grasp can occur. Because evolving contact states are only partially observable from vision and kinematics, force feedback and careful representation design become critical.
sections.details:
Robots working in real-world environments cannot assume objects are always free to pick up. Items may be stuck with glue, caked with grime, or buried under granular media. The paper defines "removal manipulation" as tasks where objects must be separated, exposed, or cleaned through contact-rich interactions such as peeling, scraping, wiping, or excavating.

The core difficulty lies in the fact that progress depends entirely on evolving contact states. Two objects may look identical visually, yet their adhesive strengths can differ by an order of magnitude. A minor variation in applied force dictates whether an object detaches cleanly or breaks completely. In short, RGB images and joint positions only offer partial observability of the underlying physical state.

Overcoming this requires a high-output hand capable of handling tens of Newtons, multi-point fingertip force sensing, and a closed-loop policy that promptly adapts trajectories in response to contact changes. Furthermore, multi-finger hands introduce a fundamental representation dilemma: fingertip sensor orientations shift constantly during motion, raising the question of how to feed raw force readings into a neural network. DexRemo tackles this by pairing a low-cost, high-force hand design with a deterministic geometric transformation that aligns forces into a wrist-centered frame.

sections.heading: Contact-Rich Manipulation and Multi-Finger Force Sensing: The State of the Art
sections.summary: Prior separation research often targeted single, isolated tasks. This work provides a standardized suite spanning detachment, cleaning, and retrieval, emphasizing the role of force coordinate frames in multimodal imitation learning.
sections.details:
### Contact-Rich Separation Tasks and Benchmarks
Conventional robotic manipulation has largely centered on unconstrained grasping. While prior studies have addressed sticker peeling, wiping, or granular scooping, most focused on single tasks or specialized jigs. Although simulation environments (such as ManiSkill3) and visuo-tactile benchmarks have emerged, standardized real-robot suites systematically evaluating physical detachment and surface removal remained lacking.

### Force Representations and Multimodal Policy Learning
Approaches for incorporating tactile or force feedback into policies include encoding tactile images or sending force targets to low-level impedance controllers. DexRemo builds on a position-based Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) backbone and investigates which coordinate frame force observations should occupy. While prior efforts (like SaTA) embed 6D sensor poses via neural networks, DexRemo applies a classical task-frame philosophy to three-axis physical force vectors, applying a deterministic geometric transformation.

### Multi-Finger Hands: Balancing Output Force and Force Sensing
Existing multi-finger platforms such as the Allegro Hand or LEAP Hand excel at grasping and in-hand manipulation, but they often lack the torque and structural stiffness needed to pry or scrape against tens of Newtons of resistance. DexRemo keeps hardware costs around $200 (adding roughly $170 per finger for sensor components) while delivering a high pull-out force of 62.5 N and exceptional power density.

sections.heading: DexRemo Hand Design and Aligning Forces to the Wrist Frame
sections.summary: The authors built a high-force three-finger hand with modular tips and integrated three-axis load-cell sensors. Using forward kinematics, measured fingertip force vectors are geometrically aligned into a shared wrist-centered frame.
sections.details:
### Characteristics of Removal and Design Requirements
Removal manipulation exhibits four primary traits: (1) history dependence, where prior contacts weaken adhesion or spread residue; (2) partial observability, as bond strength and friction are visually ambiguous; (3) multi-finger coupling, where one finger anchors while another pries; and (4) continuous force modulation, where insufficient force fails to separate and excessive force causes damage. To meet these demands, a three-finger non-collinear arrangement was selected.

### Mechanism and Teleoperation System
Each DexRemo finger features 4 degrees of freedom (IP joint, MCP joint, and a 2-DoF CMC joint) with a total finger length of 162 mm. Actuated by Feetech STS3215 servos (running at 200 Hz with under 5 ms latency), the hand pairs high-strength polymer links with aluminum housings, weighing approximately 1.8 kg. A matching passive leader device collects demonstrations, enabling intuitive bilateral-free teleoperation with on-screen 3D force vector visualization.

### Modular Fingertips and 3-Axis Force Sensing
Fingertips feature a tool-free quick-swap interface accommodating wedge-shaped rigid nail tips for prying and scraping, or compliant cleaning tips wrapped in sponges or wipes. Because the tool mount is mechanically decoupled from the sensor housing, swapping tips requires no sensor recalibration. Inside each tip, three subminiature S-beam load cells sit in an equilateral triangle. Normal force $F_z$ is obtained by summing the three cells, while in-plane forces $F_x$ and $F_y$ are recovered via a calibrated linear mapping with high precision ($R^2 > 0.986$ per axis, noise standard deviation of 0.0034 N).

### Why Transform into a Wrist-Centered Frame?
This represents the core geometric insight of the paper. Each fingertip sensor frame $\{i\}$ rotates continuously as the finger flexes and extends. Consequently, exerting an identical 10 N downward force against the environment yields completely different $[f_x, f_y, f_z]$ sensor readings depending on finger posture. If fed raw local forces, a neural network must jointly learn posture-dependent coordinate rotations and force-action mappings—a daunting task prone to spurious correlations when trained on only 20 demonstrations. DexRemo instead applies a deterministic rotation matrix ${}^w\mathbf{R}_{i,t}$ from forward kinematics:
$${}^w\mathbf{f}_{i,t} = {}^w\mathbf{R}_{i,t}\,{}^i\mathbf{f}_{i,t}$$
This ensures force components across all fingers carry a consistent geometric meaning, dramatically stabilizing learning.

sections.heading: ACT-Based Imitation Learning Fusing Force, Vision, and Pose
sections.summary: Taking multi-view RGB images, joint states, wrist-frame fingertip poses, and wrist-frame contact forces as inputs, an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) predicts joint displacement chunks. Receding-horizon execution enables real-time adaptation to changing contacts.
sections.details:
### Observation Space and Tokenization
The policy observation $\mathbf{o}_t$ combines multi-view RGB streams from three cameras (two external, one wrist-mounted), 12-DoF joint positions $\mathbf{q}_t$ and velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_t$, 21-dimensional wrist-frame fingertip poses $\mathbf{p}_t$ (positions and quaternions for three fingers), and 9-dimensional wrist-frame contact forces $\mathbf{f}_t$. Modalities are synchronized at 15 Hz. Images are tokenized via an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 backbone followed by a linear projection. Non-visual inputs (joints, poses, forces) are projected into 512-dimensional tokens using two-layer MLPs.

### Chunk Prediction and Control Loop with ACT
The policy backbone is an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT), balancing temporal smoothness with responsive control. Given an observation context length $H=1$ (the current frame only), the model predicts a chunk of future joint displacements $\Delta \hat{\mathbf{q}}_{t:t+K-1}$ over $K=100$ steps. In execution, a receding-horizon approach runs only the first $k=50$ steps (about 3.3 seconds) before re-predicting from a refreshed observation. This ensures the robot adapts quickly when an adhesive bond suddenly snaps or slippage occurs.

### Training and Demonstration Collection
For each task, only 20 successful teleoperated demonstrations were recorded under nominal conditions. Operators guided the passive leader while monitoring real-time force vectors displayed on screen. The policy is trained purely through behavior cloning conditioned on force inputs without auxiliary force prediction losses or explicit low-level force control loops. Force observations guide actions entirely through this conditioned receding-horizon mechanism.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments on 9 Tasks: The Clear Advantage of Wrist-Frame Alignment
sections.summary: Controlled ablations across six core tasks evaluated no-force, local-frame, and wrist-frame conditions. Combining wrist-frame forces with fingertip poses achieved an 83% average success rate, outperforming all baselines in stability and generalization.
sections.details:
### Task Suite and Evaluation Protocol
Experiments evaluated six core tasks across adhesive detachment (A1: barnacle detachment, A2: hot-melt glue blocks, A3: Blu-Tack putty, A4: adhered mushroom models), surface cleaning (B1: dry-erase marker on a plate), and occluded retrieval (C1: fossil models buried in gravel). Three extension scenarios were also tested: self-cleaning adhesive residue from fingertips (A5), crevice cleaning on textured silicone skin (B2), and clumping cat litter retrieval (C2). Tests incorporated held-out object shapes, colors, locations, and adhesive conditions, enforcing strict physical criteria (such as full separation or minimum cleaned surface area).

### Ablation Results: Why the Wrist Frame Matters
Across the six core tasks, six input variants were evaluated across 3 seeds and 30 trials each: (1) no sensor input $\emptyset$, (2) local force only $R$, (3) fingertip pose only $P$, (4) wrist force only $W$, (5) local force with pose $R+P$, and (6) full configuration (wrist force with pose) $P+W$.

Average success rates reached only 24% for the no-sensor baseline $\emptyset$, 38% for local force $R$, and 44% for pose alone $P$. By contrast, wrist force alone $W$ reached 58%, $R+P$ achieved 55%, and the full $P+W$ model achieved 83%. Crucially, the advantages $P+W > R+P$ and $W > R$ held across all six tasks without exception (sign test $p=0.031$). While adding raw local forces provides minor gains over vision-only baselines, aligning forces into the wrist frame provides the geometric consistency needed to generalize to unseen object configurations.

### Behavioral Quality and Force Impulse Trade-Offs
Analyzing force impulse (force integrated over time) across task families revealed meaningful distinctions. In detachment tasks (Group A), $P+W$ exhibited shorter completion times and the lowest cumulative impulse, indicating it avoided wasteful pressing and jamming by efficiently catching object edges. In surface cleaning (Group B), $P+W$ generated the highest cumulative impulse, actively pressing cleaning tips firmly against surfaces to scrub stains away. Rather than simply applying uniform pressure, the learned policy modulated force profiles to suit the physical demands of each task.

### Failure Modes and Extension Tasks
Ablation variants lacking force or using local frames suffered frequent severe failures, including losing contact, failing to hook edges, or forcefully knocking objects away. In contrast, $P+W$ virtually eliminated these errors; most of its few failures were near-complete attempts that narrowly timed out. In the extension scenarios (A5, B2, C2), the method demonstrated general efficacy, while highlighting open challenges such as finger kinematic reach limits during self-cleaning and insufficient exploratory coverage in broad granular search.

sections.heading: Discussion and Outlook: Expanding the Horizons of Physical Interaction
sections.summary: Wrist-frame force alignment serves as an effective geometric inductive bias for learning contact-rich manipulation from small demonstration sets. Future work will target full-arm integration and deeper material-level standardization.
sections.details:
### Core Insights
DexRemo demonstrates that force feedback plays an essential role in triggering transitions and adapting trajectories during contact-rich tasks like removal manipulation. The key practical insight is that multi-finger forces should be mapped into a shared wrist-centered frame rather than processed in local sensor coordinates. This inductive bias removes the need for networks to implicitly learn sensor rotations, enabling high generalization performance from a modest budget of 20 demonstrations.

### Limitations and Next Steps
Several limitations remain. First, experiments focused on localized removal behaviors within a fixed hand workspace, leaving whole-arm reaching, re-positioning, and mobile manipulation out of scope. Second, material variations in adhesives and granular media have not been fully standardized to rigorous mechanical engineering benchmarks. Third, while teleoperation offered on-screen visual force vectors, the leader lacked active haptic feedback. Promising future directions include integrating high-payload manipulator arms, incorporating high-resolution tactile skin arrays, and enabling online adaptation to uncertain material properties.

takeaways: When integrating multi-finger force measurements into imitation learning frameworks like ACT, mapping local forces into a shared wrist-centered frame via forward kinematics drastically improves generalization and sample efficiency.

With an appropriate geometric force representation and receding-horizon action chunking, robots can autonomously discover contact-driven phase transitions from just 20 teleoperated demonstrations without hand-crafted finite-state machines.

Because removal tasks (prying, scraping, excavating) exert sustained loads of tens of Newtons, hardware platforms require substantially higher force capacity, structural stiffness, and modular tool interfaces than typical grasping hands.
limitations: Focuses exclusively on local manipulation within a fixed wrist workspace, without coordinating with a robot arm for global reaching or wide-area repositioning.

Demonstration collection relies on visual force vector displays on a monitor without active bilateral haptic feedback to the operator's hands, making demonstration quality partially dependent on operator visual estimation.
Physical variations in real-world materials—such as adhesive cure states and granular moisture content—remain challenging to control and standardize rigorously across long trial runs.
